strengths: Significance: The paper addresses an important practical problem—controlling several alignment objectives across verifiable, subjective, and interactive domains—and the combined training/test-time perspective is potentially useful.

Soundness: The independently verifiable mathematics results provide some credible evidence that reward-guided search can improve accuracy; several experiments are repeated three times with standard deviations reported in the appendix.

Originality: MAH-DPO offers a simple, deployable formulation using a shared backbone and objective-specific output heads, with inference-time head mixtures that avoid retraining for each requested weighting.

Presentation and reproducibility: The framework, objectives, prompts, major hyperparameters, preference-data construction, and decoding algorithm are generally described clearly. The paper also includes an ethics statement covering consent, deidentification, storage, and dataset licensing.
weaknesses: Soundness: Most central evidence is circular. Human-values models are trained from UltraFeedback-derived preferences and evaluated using the authors' reward models trained on the same preference source. Socratic Mind training, selection, and evaluation likewise rely on simulated turns and closely related learned PRMs. Consequently, the large gains may measure optimization of the evaluator rather than improved human preferences, honesty, truthfulness, or student learning. No independent human evaluation, external evaluator, or reward-hacking analysis is provided.

Soundness: Key reported results are internally inconsistent. For Socratic Mind, Table 3 reports combined accuracy/engagement results of 0.7160/0.3800 and 0.7120/0.5420, whereas Appendix Table 9 reports 0.6659/0.3849 and 0.6514/0.5149. In Math, Table 3's engagement-guided result corresponds to the appendix condition that additionally uses an explicitly engaging system prompt, but this confound is omitted from the main-table method label. These discrepancies materially weaken the claimed training–inference synergy.

Soundness: The claim that MAH-DPO reduces cross-objective gradient interference is unsupported. Equation 9 explicitly sums all objective gradients in the shared backbone, where interference can still occur; isolating only the output heads does not establish reduced interference. No gradient-conflict measurement, ablation against equally parameterized heads, or mechanistic analysis is presented.

Soundness: The claimed controllability is weakly demonstrated. Only a few hand-selected mixtures are tested; several metric changes are non-monotonic or comparable to reported variation, and the objective-specific heads often differ only slightly. Pareto-front coverage, per-prompt control, calibration to requested weights, and statistical tests are absent.

Originality: The main ingredients are incremental: objective-specific output heads, weighted mixtures of their predictions, DPO, PRM-guided best-of-K selection, and ordinary continuation with a KV cache. The paper does not convincingly distinguish the cache method from standard incremental decoding, while the re-encoding baseline appears disadvantaged by avoidable tokenization/chat-template changes.

Methodology: Equation 5 defines a mixture of token probabilities, while the text repeatedly describes ensembling logits. The hindsight target in Equation 1 also differs from the discounted-return construction in Appendix A.1, and the computational analysis omits PRM-scoring costs and the substantial vocabulary-sized parameter and compute overhead of multiple output heads.

Evaluation: Baseline coverage is inadequate for the claimed contribution. There are no strong reward-conditioned or personalized controllable-alignment baselines, parameter-merging baselines, comparable best-of-N/search controls, or independent process/outcome-reward baselines. Compute and parameter budgets are not normalized, so improvements cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed factorization.

Presentation: Several interpretations overstate the tables—for example, the paper claims limited non-target degradation although math accuracy guidance substantially reduces engagement and Socratic accuracy guidance reduces engagement. Math engagement is also strongly tied to stylistic prompts and a judge calibrated on only 200 labeled responses at 75.8% accuracy, making the very large engagement gains questionable.

Reproducibility: The abstract's code link is blank. Exact evaluation sample sizes and splits, random seeds, hardware/compute, implementation details for MODPO and head mixing, judge calibration procedure, and generated training/evaluation artifacts are not fully specified. Three-run standard deviations do not substitute for significance testing over evaluation examples.

Limitations and ethics: Despite stating that remaining limitations are reported, the manuscript has no substantive limitations discussion. It does not analyze evaluator bias, reward hacking, simulator validity, generalization beyond two base-model families, privacy/licensing details for released dialogue derivatives, or the gap between a learned engagement proxy and actual student learning. The ethics statement is welcome but does not resolve these material deployment risks.

strengths: Significance: Multi-objective alignment with inference-time control is an important problem, and studying verifiable, subjective, and interactive objectives within one framework is potentially useful.
Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished. The appendices provide system prompts, many hyperparameters, and standard deviations over three runs.
The experiments cover three distinct settings—MATH, UltraFeedback, and Socratic Mind—and compare training-time, decoding-time, and combined approaches.
The reported results suggest that specialized output heads and reward-guided search can move measured objectives in targeted directions, motivating further study.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central evaluation is substantially circular. Human-values outputs are evaluated using trained reward models closely tied to the same preference data and objectives used for training. Socratic Mind training and evaluation likewise rely on PRMs distilled from GPT-4o labels and simulated student turns. Selecting outputs to maximize these models and then reporting those models' scores does not establish improved human preference, honesty, truthfulness, engagement, or tutoring quality; it may primarily measure reward-model exploitation. No independent human evaluation or sufficiently independent external evaluator breaks this loop.

The subjective evaluators are weakly validated. The MATH engagement judge reaches only 75.8% accuracy on 200 human-labeled, prompt-constructed responses, while the Socratic engagement judge has only 66% test accuracy on 80 examples. Nevertheless, these noisy signals support large downstream claims. Inter-annotator agreement, annotation protocol, uncertainty propagation, and human evaluation of final systems are absent.

The MATH split description raises a serious contamination concern: Appendix B calls approximately 12,000 problems the 'MATH training dataset,' although MATH has 12,500 examples in total rather than in its standard training split. The manuscript never states the final evaluation split or its size, so it is impossible to rule out train-test overlap.

Originality is limited and insufficiently isolated. MAH-DPO is essentially separate vocabulary projection heads trained with per-head DPO losses over a shared backbone. The claimed reduction in gradient interference is not demonstrated: all objectives still update the shared backbone, and there are no gradient-conflict measurements, capacity-matched multi-head controls, or ablations separating extra parameters from the proposed routing.

Several claims overstate the tables. On Socratic Mind, MAH-DPO loses accuracy relative to Single-Head DPO and MODPO while only marginally improving engagement over Single-Head DPO. The purportedly specialized truth head is not best on truthfulness, and mixtures often improve all human-value metrics, which does not demonstrate disentangled heads. The weight sweeps are sparse, partly non-monotonic, and overlap in standard deviation, so they do not establish 'smooth' fine-grained control or an expanded Pareto frontier.

The continuing-hidden-state contribution is weakly founded. Exact causal decoding from an accumulated token sequence and decoding from its KV cache should be equivalent apart from numerical effects; the large degradation of the text-concatenation baseline suggests changes in chat templating, tokenization, or implementation rather than an intrinsic discontinuity. The paper does not specify this baseline sufficiently, compare against standard cached decoding/search systems, or provide latency and memory measurements supporting its complexity claims.

Important technical details are inconsistent. Equation 4 conditions prediction of y_t on y_{1:t}; Equation 5 mixes probabilities, whereas the experiments describe combining logits. Equation 1 defines a one-step reward plus discounted terminal outcome, while Appendix A instead describes a discounted return over future rewards. Calling the method 'vectorized reward' is also misleading because the implementation uses routed scalar losses and separate heads rather than a clearly defined vector-valued optimization.

The baselines are inadequate for the breadth of the claims. Test-time experiments omit strong best-of-N, reward-guided search, outcome-reward, and multi-objective decoding baselines. Training experiments lack a capacity-matched multi-head baseline and personalized/conditioned multi-objective methods. Compute, parameter, and serving costs of adding multiple full vocabulary projection matrices are not quantified.

Reproducibility is not adequate despite the appendix. The promised code URL is blank, and the manuscript omits exact evaluation sample sizes and splits, random seeds, hardware and compute budgets, optimizer/scheduler details, complete MODPO settings, calibration procedures, and several evaluation prompts. These omissions are especially consequential given the possible MATH leakage and evaluator dependence.

Ethics and limitations treatment is incomplete. The consent, IRB, deidentification, and licensing statements are positive, but the paper claims to report remaining limitations without actually providing a limitations section. It does not seriously discuss reward hacking, evaluator bias, unreliable notions of engagement, risks of optimizing tutors against simulated students, or the consequences of treating subjective values as separable controllable axes. strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: controlling several alignment objectives without training a separate model for every preference combination. The coverage of verifiable, subjective, and interactive domains is ambitious and potentially significant.

MAH-DPO is a simple, practical architecture: objective-specific output heads share an LLM backbone, can be trained jointly, and permit inexpensive inference-time interpolation. The comparison with SFT, single-head DPO, and MODPO shows promising gains, particularly for mathematical engagement and the UltraFeedback dimensions.

The combination of training-time specialization and test-time reward-guided selection is useful. Several results are sizable—for example, the math ensemble improves engagement from 0.7367 for MODPO to 0.8733, while value-guided decoding raises accuracy to approximately 0.80.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. Algorithms, prompts, preference-data construction, hyperparameters, and standard deviations over three runs are supplied, and the visual presentation is polished.

The ethics statement appropriately describes consent, IRB review, deidentification, restricted access, and licensing for the tutoring data. I found no unresolved ethical issue that alone would preclude publication.
weaknesses: The central non-verifiable-domain evidence is substantially circular. Human-values reward models are trained from UltraFeedback and then used to evaluate models optimized using closely related preference signals. Socratic Mind responses are optimized and evaluated with PRMs trained largely from LLM-generated labels and simulated student turns. There is no independent human evaluation or sufficiently independent judge, so the reported improvements may primarily demonstrate reward-model optimization rather than genuine gains in honesty, truthfulness, engagement, or tutoring quality.

The reliability of the subjective supervision is weak. The math engagement judge reaches only 75.8% agreement on 200 human-labeled responses, while the Socratic engagement judge has 0.66 test accuracy and the resulting accuracy PRM only 0.70. Downstream score differences are nevertheless interpreted as substantive behavioral improvements without uncertainty propagation, judge-bias analysis, or reward-hacking checks.

Several reported results are inconsistent. For Socratic Mind, Table 3 reports combined accuracy/engagement results of 0.7160/0.3800 and 0.7120/0.5420, whereas Table 9 reports 0.6659/0.3849 and 0.6514/0.5149. Table 4's generic “PRM-guided” row combines the accuracy-guided accuracy value with the engagement-guided engagement value from Table 2. These are material discrepancies in headline evidence.

The claimed reduction in cross-objective gradient interference is not established. Objective heads are isolated, but the shared backbone still receives the sum of all objective gradients. The paper provides neither gradient-conflict measurements nor an ablation separating the effect of multiple heads from data, capacity, optimization, or ensembling.

The purported contribution of “continuing hidden state” is questionable. Carrying the KV cache is standard autoregressive decoding; re-encoding the identical token sequence with identical positions should reproduce the same transformer state apart from numerical effects. The large degradation of the text-concatenation baseline likely reflects retokenization or formatting artifacts that a properly implemented token-ID baseline would avoid. Thus the comparison does not substantiate the claimed algorithmic advantage.

The proposed standardized PRM framework is more a taxonomy of heuristics than a validated general method. In Case C, an outcome reward model trained on complete responses is simply applied to partial responses—the same granularity mismatch criticized in the introduction—and no experiment establishes that these prefix scores are calibrated or meaningful.

Claims of smooth control and an expanded Pareto frontier are overstated. Only a small number of fixed mixtures are evaluated, some curves are non-monotonic, and there is no formal Pareto analysis. Several “combined” math results also use an explicit engaging system prompt, confounding head weighting or PRM guidance with prompt steering.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the appendices: evaluation sample counts, exact splits, seeds, objective weights, head-ensemble implementation (the text alternates between mixing logits and probabilities), compute requirements, annotation protocol and agreement, and several decoding/value-blending parameters are missing. The promised code URL is blank.

The paper contains no substantive limitations section despite claiming that remaining limitations are reported. Important limitations—proxy-reward validity, simulated rather than real student outcomes, reward hacking, judge dependence, and added test-time cost from five candidates per step—are not discussed. Overall, the idea is promising, but independent evaluation and correction of the experimental record are necessary before the central claims can be relied upon.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: jointly controlling multiple alignment objectives spanning verifiable reasoning, subjective preferences, and interactive tutoring.

MAH-DPO is a simple, understandable design: objective-specific output heads isolate head-level gradients while sharing the expensive backbone, and inference-time logit mixing offers lightweight control without retraining.

The experimental scope is broad. The manuscript evaluates math, human values, and tutoring; compares against SFT, single-head DPO, MODPO, parameter merging, and a PPO baseline; and includes segmentation, reward-noise, latency, objective-conflict, and five-head scaling analyses.

The appendices provide many useful implementation details, prompts, standard deviations, data-construction procedures, and an explicit discussion of participant consent, IRB review, privacy, licensing, and data access.

The limited independent evaluation is encouraging: three human annotators consistently prefer MAH-DPO for math engagement, and a GPT-4o evaluator reproduces the direction of the engagement improvement.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is substantially circular. Human-values reward models are trained from UltraFeedback dimension labels and then used to evaluate optimization against those dimensions; Socratic Mind candidates are likewise generated, selected, and evaluated largely through learned judges/PRMs. Independent human validation is provided only for math engagement on 100 problems, with merely moderate agreement (77%, Cohen's kappa 0.45). Thus large reported gains may partly reflect reward-model exploitation rather than genuine alignment.

There are material inconsistencies in the reported results. For Socratic Mind, Table 5 reports combined accuracy/engagement of 0.7160/0.3800 and 0.7120/0.5420, whereas Appendix Table 18 reports 0.6659/0.3849 and 0.6514/0.5149 for the nominally corresponding methods. Table 8 also reports one generic PRM-guided row with accuracy 0.7633 and engagement 0.7187, although Table 16 shows these values come from different accuracy-guided and engagement-guided configurations. These discrepancies undermine the main synergy claims.

The claimed cross-domain generalization of the unified PRM is not demonstrated: it is trained on a mixture containing all seven evaluated dimensions and tested on those same domains. This establishes multi-domain training, not transfer to an unseen domain or objective. The unified binary classifier also lacks an explicit objective-conditioning variable, making its interpretation as a controllable multi-objective PRM unclear.

The motivation for 'continuing hidden-state' decoding is technically questionable. Re-encoding exactly the same token sequence in deterministic evaluation should reproduce the same transformer representations; whitespace, tokenization, and special-token differences arise only if the reconstruction changes the sequence. The manuscript therefore appears to compare cached decoding with a lossy or differently formatted reconstruction, rather than establishing a representational advantage. KV caching itself is standard, so the associated originality claim is weak.

The non-verifiable 'PRM' framework is conceptually loose. Case C simply applies a response-level Bradley-Terry reward model to partial text, precisely the granularity mismatch highlighted in the introduction. No evidence establishes that these scores are calibrated process rewards or that local selection produces better final human judgments.

Evidence for fine-grained objective control is limited. Only a few interpolation weights are tested; several curves are weak or non-monotonic, and most objectives are positively correlated. Although one helpfulness-honesty conflict subset is included, there is no Pareto-quality, hypervolume, or matched-compute analysis showing that logit interpolation reliably spans trade-offs better than established conditional or decoding-time control methods.

Baseline fairness and significance are insufficiently established. The paper does not compare against several closely related controllable multi-objective approaches discussed in its own related work, and it gives limited evidence that baseline hyperparameters and compute were comparably optimized. The main method is also a fairly direct combination of multiple language-model heads, per-head DPO, best-of-K reward selection, and KV caching.

Some conclusions overstate the results. Targeted guidance does cause meaningful collateral degradation—for example, math accuracy guidance lowers engagement from 0.5133 to 0.4553, while Socratic accuracy guidance lowers engagement from 0.3407 to 0.2660. The claim that non-target objectives remain close and that the Pareto frontier is expanded is not supported by a formal frontier comparison.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite detailed appendices: the abstract's 'code is available at' field is blank, exact evaluation splits and all evaluator checkpoints are not consistently identified, and the annotation protocol lacks demographic, compensation, and recruitment details. The reported three-run standard deviations do not substitute for uncertainty over prompts or human examples.

The ethics discussion appropriately covers consent, privacy, and licensing, but the impact statement treats user-adjustable value weights mainly as beneficial. It does not adequately analyze misuse, unsafe objective combinations, reward hacking, or governance of who selects objectives in sensitive educational and public-facing deployments.

strengths: Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized and clearly explains the three-part MAHALO framework, with useful algorithms, prompts, hyperparameters, and standard deviations. Significance: Controllable multi-objective alignment spanning mathematical reasoning, human values, and tutoring is an important practical problem, and combining training-time specialization with test-time steering is potentially useful.
Soundness: The mathematical-accuracy experiments use objectively checkable outcomes and show a substantial test-time improvement, from 0.6853 to 0.7993 accuracy with value guidance.

The evaluation is broader than a typical proof of concept: it includes three domains, several training baselines, three-seed variability, segmentation and PRM-noise ablations, a conflict subset, and limited cross-model and human validation of math engagement.
Ethics: The appendix reports IRB review where applicable, consent, de-identification, encrypted storage, restricted access, and licensing/privacy precautions for the tutoring data.
weaknesses: Soundness: Much of the central evidence is circular. In Human Values, reward models trained from UltraFeedback dimensions are used to evaluate methods optimized on those same dimensions. In Socratic Mind, PRMs label the DPO pairs and then score the resulting models. PRM-guided decoding explicitly selects candidates using these evaluators, so higher evaluator scores do not establish improved human preferences. Independent human evaluation is provided only for math engagement, on 100 problems, with merely moderate agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.45).

The test-time evaluation lacks essential compute-matched baselines such as best-of-K with random selection, outcome-reward selection, or competitive methods such as ARGS/PARM. Comparing repeated best-of-five selection against one unguided generation cannot isolate the contribution of the proposed PRMs or establish state-of-the-art test-time alignment.

The claimed hidden-state contribution is conceptually questionable. Correctly re-encoding the identical token IDs with identical positions and attention should reproduce autoregressive states up to numerical error; tokenization or special-token changes indicate an avoidable implementation mismatch. The severe degradation of the paper's text-chunk baseline in Human Values therefore appears to reflect a flawed re-encoding baseline. Carrying a KV cache is also standard autoregressive generation, limiting originality.

Several headline conclusions overstate the tables. Targeted guidance does cause meaningful interference: math accuracy guidance reduces engagement from 0.5133 to 0.4553, and Socratic accuracy guidance reduces engagement from 0.3380 to 0.2660. Moreover, the main-table math 'synergy' result for engagement uses a special engaging system prompt; under the normal prompt, engagement falls from 0.8733 for MAH-DPO alone to 0.6813 after engagement-guided decoding.

There is a material results inconsistency: Table 5 reports Socratic MAH-DPO plus accuracy guidance as 0.7160/0.3800 and plus engagement guidance as 0.7120/0.5420, whereas Appendix Table 18 reports 0.6659/0.3849 and 0.6514/0.5149. These differences are far beyond rounding and undermine reproducibility.

The 'unified PRM transferability' claim is unsupported: the PRM is trained on a mixture containing all seven evaluated domain-objective combinations and then tested on those same domains. This demonstrates multitask fitting, not transfer to a held-out domain or objective.

The evidence for inference-time control and reduced interference is weak. In Math, head weighting changes engagement only from 0.8667 to 0.8840 and accuracy changes are often within seed variability. The backbone still receives summed gradients from every objective, so only the output heads—not the overall model—are gradient-isolated. No direct gradient-conflict or matched-capacity ablation supports the proposed mechanism.

Originality is limited. Separate vocabulary heads are a conventional multitask architecture, logit interpolation is standard, and PRM-guided best-of-K decoding is established. The three non-verifiable 'cases' are primarily a taxonomy: Case C applies an outcome-trained reward model to prefixes, retaining the very granularity mismatch the paper identifies.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the breadth of the claims. The stated code URL is blank; seeds and complete split construction are missing; Equation 1 defines a current-step reward plus discounted terminal reward, while Appendix A describes a full discounted return; and the value-guidance interpolation coefficient is unspecified. Full vocabulary projections are also large, while overhead is reported only for two heads despite claims based on a five-head model.

Limitations and ethics treatment is incomplete. There is no substantive limitations section addressing reward hacking, evaluator dependence, cultural subjectivity of 'human values,' deployment risks of user-controlled objective weights, or the weak tutoring judges (reported test accuracies of 0.66 and 0.70). The generic impact statement instead makes broad claims about fairness, inclusion, and pluralism that the experiments do not evaluate.

Overall, the paper targets an important problem and contains promising engineering, but circular evaluation, missing test-time controls, confounded comparisons, inconsistent reported results, and unsupported mechanistic and transfer claims prevent the methodology and evidence from supporting its central conclusions. These are acceptance-blocking issues rather than minor revisions.

strengths: Soundness: The evaluation is broad and generally well designed, spanning verifiable mathematics, subjective human-value dimensions, and multi-turn tutoring. Comparisons include SFT, single-head DPO, MODPO, DPO Soup, and a PPO baseline, with three-run standard deviations and useful conflict, segmentation, PRM-noise, and objective-scaling analyses.

Empirical results are consistently promising. For example, MAH-DPO improves all three Human Values scores over MODPO, and combining MAH-DPO with accuracy value guidance raises Math accuracy from 0.7247 to 0.8000 while largely retaining the training-time engagement gain.

Significance: A single shared model with objective-specific heads, inference-time logit mixing, and optional PRM-guided search is practically useful. It provides a plausible alternative to storing separate aligned models or retraining for every preference weighting.

Originality: Although the individual ingredients are familiar, their integration into objective-specific DPO heads with inference-time mixtures and cross-domain PRM guidance is a meaningful systems contribution. The experiments also provide useful evidence about when training-time versus test-time alignment is most effective.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper is clearly organized and supplies substantial implementation detail, including dataset construction, prompts, hyperparameters, decoding parameters, reward-model training, computational measurements, and full standard deviations.

Ethics: The manuscript reports IRB review and consent where applicable, de-identification and restricted handling of tutoring dialogues, dataset-license considerations, and limits on releasing sensitive data. It also acknowledges evaluator uncertainty and the need for larger human studies.
weaknesses: Soundness is limited by substantial proxy-evaluation circularity. Human Values performance is measured with learned reward models closely tied to the same annotation source used for alignment, while Socratic Mind preferences and final metrics depend on trained PRMs and simulated student turns. These experiments establish optimization of the proxies more convincingly than improvement in human preferences or learning outcomes.

The human validation is too small to resolve this concern. On 100 Math problems, agreement between the Qwen judge and human majority is only 77% with Cohen's kappa of 0.45, and individual estimates of base-model engagement range from 39% to 80%. No comparable human validation is given for Human Values or tutoring, where the proxy concerns are stronger.

There is a material numerical inconsistency: the Socratic Mind combined results in main Table 5 are 0.7160/0.3800 and 0.7120/0.5420, whereas Appendix Table 18 reports 0.6659/0.3849 and 0.6514/0.5149 for the ostensibly corresponding configurations. This undermines the claimed training/test-time synergy until the evaluation protocol and correct values are clarified.

The Math synergy result is confounded: Appendix Table 16 reveals that the reported 0.9060 engagement for MAH-DPO plus engagement guidance also uses an explicit engaging system prompt, although main Table 5 labels the method only as MAH-DPO plus Engaging PRM. A matched MAH-DPO baseline under that prompt is needed to attribute the gain to PRM guidance.

The continuing-hidden-state contribution is conceptually overstated. Re-encoding exactly the same token IDs with the same positions and attention mask should reproduce cached autoregressive decoding up to numerical error; the stated discrepancies arise from text reconstruction, tokenization, whitespace, or special-token changes. Thus the quality comparison appears to expose an avoidable implementation artifact, while the latency improvement is largely standard KV caching. An exact token-ID re-encoding baseline is needed.

Claims of limited interference are stronger than the results support. Math accuracy guidance reduces engagement from 0.5133 to 0.4720, and Socratic accuracy guidance reduces engagement from 0.3380 to 0.2660. Moreover, separate heads isolate output-layer gradients but not conflicting gradients in the shared backbone, as Equation 7 itself shows.

The proposed standardized treatment of non-verifiable tasks is partly heuristic. Case C scores incomplete generations using a reward model trained on complete responses—the same granularity mismatch criticized in the introduction—without directly validating calibration on partial prefixes.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the detailed appendix: the displayed code link is empty, exact split identifiers and seeds are not supplied, and storage/training costs are reported only for a two-head configuration despite experiments with five full vocabulary projection heads. The paper also lacks a focused limitations discussion of proxy reward hacking and risks from exposing controls over honesty or truthfulness.
